Name: Buddhism (Theravada)
Description: The oldest surviving branch of Buddhism, emphasizing individual enlightenment through the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
CreationMyth: Buddhist cosmology describes cycles of creation and destruction (kalpas) rather than a single creation event. The universe arises from collective karma.
CorePrinciples: Four Noble Truths: Life involves suffering, suffering arises from craving, suffering can cease, the path to cessation is the Eightfold Path
Anatta (no-self): There is no permanent, unchanging self
Anicca (impermanence): All conditioned things are impermanent
Karma: Actions have consequences across lifetimes
Nirvana: Liberation from the cycle of rebirth

Name: Christianity (Catholic)
Description: The largest Christian denomination, emphasizing apostolic succession, sacraments, and the authority of the Pope.
CreationMyth: God created the universe in six days and rested on the seventh. Humans were created in God's image, fell from grace through original sin, and await redemption.
CorePrinciples: Trinity: One God in three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit)
Salvation through Jesus Christ's death and resurrection
Seven Sacraments as means of grace
Papal infallibility in matters of faith and morals
Natural law and moral theology
Social justice and preferential option for the poor

Name: Islam (Sunni)
Description: The largest denomination of Islam, following the Sunnah (practices) of Muhammad and the first four caliphs.
Sources: Four schools of jurisprudence (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali)
CreationMyth: Allah created the heavens and earth in six days. Adam was created from clay, and all humans descend from Adam and Eve.
CorePrinciples: Tawhid: Absolute monotheism - Allah is one and indivisible
Five Pillars: Shahada (faith), Salat (prayer), Zakat (charity), Sawm (fasting), Hajj (pilgrimage)
Prophets: Muhammad is the final prophet in a line including Abraham, Moses, and Jesus
Quran is the literal word of God
Sharia: Divine law governing all aspects of life
Ummah: Universal Muslim community

Name: Hinduism (Advaita Vedanta)
Era: 8th century CE - Present (philosophy); roots in 1500 BCE (Vedas)
Description: Non-dualistic school of Hindu philosophy teaching that Brahman (ultimate reality) and Atman (individual soul) are identical.
CreationMyth: Creation is cyclical, emerging from Brahman through Maya (cosmic illusion). The universe undergoes endless cycles of creation and dissolution.
CorePrinciples: Brahman: Ultimate, unchanging reality
Maya: The illusory nature of the material world
Atman = Brahman: Individual consciousness is identical to universal consciousness
Moksha: Liberation through realization of one's true nature
Karma and reincarnation
Jnana Yoga: Path of knowledge and self-inquiry

Name: Taoism
Description: Chinese philosophical and religious tradition emphasizing living in harmony with the Tao (the Way).
CreationMyth: The Tao is the source of all existence. From the Tao came the One, from the One came Yin and Yang, from these came all things.
CorePrinciples: Tao: The fundamental nature of the universe
Wu wei: Non-action or effortless action in harmony with natural flow
Yin and Yang: Complementary opposites in dynamic balance
Simplicity and naturalness
Non-attachment to outcomes
Three Treasures: compassion, frugality, humility

Name: Judaism (Orthodox)
Description: Traditional form of Judaism adhering strictly to Torah law and rabbinic interpretations.
CreationMyth: God created the world in six days. Humans are created in God's image and given dominion over the earth. Jews are God's chosen people with whom He made a covenant.
CorePrinciples: Monotheism: One God, creator of the universe
Torah as divine revelation
613 Mitzvot (commandments)
Covenant between God and the Jewish people
Messiah will come to redeem Israel
Importance of study, prayer, and observance
Tikkun Olam: Repairing the world

Name: Confucianism
Description: Chinese ethical and philosophical system emphasizing moral cultivation, social harmony, and proper conduct.
CorePrinciples: Ren (仁): Humaneness, benevolence
Li (禮): Ritual propriety, proper conduct
Filial piety: Respect for parents and ancestors
Five Relationships: ruler-subject, father-son, husband-wife, elder-younger, friend-friend
Junzi: The ideal of the cultivated person
Education and self-cultivation
Meritocracy in governance

Name: Stoicism
Description: Ancient Greek philosophy teaching that virtue, reason, and living in accordance with nature lead to eudaimonia (flourishing).
CorePrinciples: Dichotomy of control: Focus only on what you can control
Virtue is the sole good; vice is the sole evil
Living according to nature and reason
Apatheia: Freedom from destructive emotions
Amor fati: Love of one's fate
Cosmopolitanism: All humans are part of one universal community
Memento mori: Remember death

Name: Secular Humanism
Description: Non-religious philosophy affirming human dignity, reason, ethics, and justice without supernatural beliefs.
CorePrinciples: No supernatural or divine authority
Human reason and science as tools for understanding
Ethical values derived from human experience and empathy
Individual autonomy and freedom of thought
Democratic values and human rights
Social responsibility and altruism
Critical thinking and skepticism

Name: Indigenous Australian Dreamtime
Description: Aboriginal Australian spiritual framework where ancestral beings created the land and established law and culture.
CreationMyth: During the Dreamtime, ancestral spirits rose from the earth and sky, creating the land, animals, plants, and people. These beings established the laws and customs before transforming into features of the landscape.
CorePrinciples: All life is interconnected
Land is sacred and holds ancestral presence
Custodianship rather than ownership of land
Circular time: past, present, and future coexist
Knowledge transmitted through story, song, and ceremony
Kinship systems define social responsibilities
Balance and harmony with nature

Name: Islam (Shia)
Description: The second-largest branch of Islam, emphasizing the spiritual and political authority of Ali and the Imams as rightful successors to the Prophet Muhammad.
CreationMyth: Shares Islamic cosmology: Allah created the heavens and earth. Adam created from clay; all humans descend from Adam and Eve.
CorePrinciples: Imamate: Divine authority vested in Ali and eleven descendants
Occultation: Twelfth Imam is hidden, will return as Mahdi
Five Pillars of Islam plus five additional principles (Usul al-Din)
Tawassul: Intercession through Imams and saints
Lamentation and commemoration of martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala
Ijtihad: Ongoing religious interpretation by qualified scholars (marjas)
Justice (Adl) as a divine attribute and human obligation

Name: Islam (Sufism)
Description: The mystical dimension of Islam emphasizing direct personal experience of the Divine, love, and inner purification of the soul.
CorePrinciples: Tariqa: Spiritual path to direct knowledge of God
Dhikr: Remembrance and repetition of divine names
Fana: Annihilation of the ego in God
Baqa: Subsistence in God after annihilation
Murshid: Spiritual guide essential for the path
Love as the supreme path to the divine
Sama: Spiritual music and movement as devotional practice
Inner meaning beneath outer religious law

Name: Buddhism (Mahayana)
Description: The largest Buddhist tradition, emphasizing the bodhisattva ideal of compassion for all beings and the aspiration to achieve full Buddhahood for the benefit of all.
CorePrinciples: Bodhisattva ideal: delay personal nirvana to help all beings
Sunyata: Emptiness of inherent existence in all phenomena
Buddha-nature: All beings possess the seed of enlightenment
Skillful means (upaya): Teachings adapted to listeners' capacity
Trikaya: Three bodies of the Buddha (Dharmakaya, Sambhogakaya, Nirmanakaya)
Interconnectedness of all phenomena (Indra's net)
Compassion (karuna) and wisdom (prajna) as twin pillars

Name: Buddhism (Vajrayana/Tibetan)
Description: Tantric Buddhism practiced in Tibet, Mongolia, and the Himalayan region, using ritual, visualization, and esoteric methods to accelerate the path to enlightenment.
Sources: Tibetan Book of the Dead (Bardo Thodol)
CorePrinciples: Tantra: Esoteric methods using body, speech, and mind in practice
Guru-yoga: Complete devotion to the qualified lama
Deity yoga: Visualization of oneself as an enlightened being
Rigpa: Recognition of the nature of mind as pure awareness
Tulku system: Reincarnated lamas preserve lineage
Bardo teachings: Navigation of consciousness after death
Compassion and emptiness inseparably united

Name: Buddhism (Zen/Chan)
Description: A school of Mahayana Buddhism emphasizing direct experience of enlightenment through meditation, koans, and the teacher-student relationship, rather than scriptural study.
Sources: Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
CorePrinciples: Zazen: Sitting meditation as primary practice
Kensho/Satori: Direct insight into one's true nature
Koans: Paradoxical riddles to break conceptual thinking
Direct mind-to-mind transmission beyond words
Everyday life as practice (chopping wood, carrying water)
Beginner's mind: approach each moment fresh
Non-attachment to concepts, even Buddhist ones

Name: Sikhism
Description: Monotheistic religion founded by Guru Nanak in Punjab, emphasizing equality of all people, service to others, and devotional remembrance of the one God.
CorePrinciples: Ik Onkar: There is only one God
Equality of all humans regardless of caste, gender, or religion
Nam Japna: Meditation on God's name
Kirat Karni: Honest labor and earning
Vand Chhakna: Sharing with those in need
Seva: Selfless service to the community
Langar: Community kitchen open to all, regardless of background
Rejection of ritual, superstition, and idol worship
NotableFigures: Guru Gobind Singh Ji (tenth and last human Guru)

Name: Hinduism (Vaishnavism)
Description: The largest Hindu denomination, centered on devotion to Vishnu and his avatars, especially Rama and Krishna, emphasizing bhakti (loving devotion) as the primary path.
CorePrinciples: Bhakti: Personal devotion and love for God as highest path
Vishnu as the supreme personal God, sustainer of the universe
Avatars: God descends into the world to restore dharma
Surrender (prapatti) to God's grace for liberation
Devotional practices: singing, chanting, pilgrimage, image worship
Vaishnava ethics: non-violence, vegetarianism, purity
God is both transcendent and immanent

Name: Hinduism (Shaivism)
Description: Major Hindu tradition centered on devotion to Shiva as the supreme being, encompassing diverse schools from devotional bhakti to the non-dual Kashmir Shaivism.
CorePrinciples: Shiva as the supreme reality, both destroyer and regenerator
Shakti: Divine feminine energy inseparable from Shiva
Liberation through recognition of one's identity with Shiva
Pashupati: Shiva as lord of souls and the universe
Yogic practice and asceticism as paths to liberation
Kashmir Shaivism: Universe is the free play of divine consciousness
Ritual worship, mantra, and tantra as vehicles of liberation

Name: Jainism
Description: Ancient Indian religion emphasizing non-violence, truth, non-attachment, and individual liberation through rigorous ethical practice.
CorePrinciples: Ahimsa: Radical non-violence toward all living beings
Anekantavada: Many-sidedness of reality; no single perspective is complete
Aparigraha: Non-possessiveness and limiting attachments
Satya: Truth
Five vows (Mahavratas for monks, Anuvratas for laypersons)
Karma as physical substance binding the soul
Liberation (moksha) through purification and ascetic practice
No creator god; universe is eternal and self-regulating

Name: Zoroastrianism
Description: One of the world's oldest monotheistic religions, teaching the cosmic struggle between truth and lie, and the importance of good thoughts, words, and deeds.
CreationMyth: Ahura Mazda, the supreme god, created the world as a perfect spiritual realm, then a material counterpart. Angra Mainyu (Ahriman), the destructive spirit, invaded the material creation introducing evil, death, and suffering. History is the cosmic battle between these principles, ending with a final renovation (Frashokereti) when evil is defeated.
CorePrinciples: Ahura Mazda: The one, wise, good God
Dualism: Cosmic struggle between Ahura Mazda (good) and Angra Mainyu (evil)
Asha: Truth, righteousness, cosmic order
Druj: Lie, chaos, evil
Good thoughts, good words, good deeds (Humata, Hukhta, Hvarshta)
Human free will to choose between good and evil
Frashokereti: Final renovation and restoration of perfect world
Yazatas (divine beings) assist Ahura Mazda

Name: Shinto
Description: Indigenous Japanese religion focusing on kami (spirits inhabiting all things), ritual purity, ancestor veneration, and the inseparability of humans and nature.
CreationMyth: In the beginning, the heavens and earth were mixed chaos. Three invisible deities appeared spontaneously. Later, the divine couple Izanagi and Izanami stood on the floating bridge of heaven and stirred the ocean with a jeweled spear, creating the first island. They then gave birth to the Japanese islands and many kami. Izanami died giving birth to the fire god; Izanagi retrieved her from Yomi (underworld) but she had eaten there, making her unable to return. When Izanagi cleansed himself, Amaterasu (sun goddess) was born from his left eye, Tsukuyomi (moon god) from his right, and Susanoo (storm god) from his nose.
CorePrinciples: Kami: Spirits residing in natural phenomena, ancestors, exceptional people
Kannagara: Living in harmony with the divine order of nature
Harae: Ritual purification removes pollution (kegare)
Makoto: Sincerity and truthfulness
Musubi: Creative and harmonizing power binding people to kami
Ancestor veneration through household shrines
Japan as sacred land; emperor as descendant of Amaterasu
This world, not afterlife, is primary concern

Name: Bahá'í Faith
Description: Independent world religion teaching the unity of God, religion, and humanity, emphasizing progressive revelation and the establishment of a peaceful global civilization.
Sources: Writings of the Báb and Abdu'l-Bahá
CorePrinciples: Unity of God: All religions worship the same God
Unity of religion: All major religions are successive chapters of one revelation
Unity of humanity: All humans are one people
Independent investigation of truth
Harmony of science and religion
Equality of men and women
Elimination of all forms of prejudice
Progressive revelation: God continues to send messengers as humanity evolves

Name: Judaism (Reform)
Description: Liberal Jewish denomination emphasizing adaptation of Jewish tradition to modern life, gender equality, and personal autonomy in religious observance.
CorePrinciples: Torah as human document inspired by God, subject to interpretation
Ethical monotheism over ritual observance
Religious practice adapted to contemporary life
Gender equality in all religious roles
Tikkun Olam: Social justice as core Jewish obligation
Welcoming of interfaith families and LGBTQ+ individuals
Zionism and support for Israel as part of Jewish identity (debated)

Name: Judaism (Kabbalah/Mysticism)
Description: The mystical tradition within Judaism, seeking to understand the hidden dimensions of God, the universe, and the soul through esoteric study and spiritual practice.
Sources: Etz Chaim (Tree of Life, Lurianic Kabbalah)
Works of the Ari (Rabbi Isaac Luria)
CorePrinciples: Ein Sof: God as infinite, beyond all description
Ten Sefirot: Divine emanations through which God interacts with creation
Four Worlds: levels of reality from divine to material
Tikkun Olam: Cosmic repair through righteous acts
Soul has multiple levels: Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chaya, Yechida
Gematria: Numerical values of letters reveal hidden meanings
Shevirat ha-Kelim: The shattering of the vessels and the task of repair
NotableFigures: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (attributed author of Zohar)

Name: Christianity (Eastern Orthodox)
Description: The ancient Christian church of the Eastern Roman Empire, emphasizing theosis (divinization), tradition, icons, and conciliar authority rather than papal supremacy.
Sources: Church Fathers (Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, John Chrysostom)
CorePrinciples: Theosis: Union with God as the purpose of human existence
Tradition: Scripture and holy tradition as co-equal sources
Icons as windows to the divine, not idols
Apophatic theology: God's essence is unknowable
Conciliar authority: councils of bishops, not a single pope
Liturgical worship as participation in heaven on earth
Synergy: Human will cooperates with divine grace in salvation

Name: Christianity (Protestant/Evangelical)
Description: The family of Christian traditions arising from the Reformation, emphasizing Scripture alone, faith alone, and grace alone, with evangelical branches stressing personal conversion and mission.
Sources: Calvin's Institutes of the Christian Religion
CorePrinciples: Sola Scriptura: Bible is the sole authority for faith and practice
Sola Fide: Salvation by faith alone
Sola Gratia: Salvation by grace alone, not works
Priesthood of all believers: Direct access to God for all
Personal conversion and born-again experience (evangelical)
Great Commission: Active missionary work globally
Predestination (Calvinist traditions)

Name: Christianity (Mormonism/LDS)
Description: Restorationist Christian denomination founded by Joseph Smith, claiming a restoration of original Christianity through new scripture and prophetic authority.
CorePrinciples: Restoration: True Christianity lost and restored through Joseph Smith
Continuing revelation through living prophets
Exaltation: Humans can progress toward divine status
Pre-mortal existence of all souls
Families sealed for eternity through temple ordinances
Plan of Salvation: Pre-mortal life, mortality, afterlife
Word of Wisdom: Health code including abstinence from alcohol, tobacco, coffee
NotableFigures: Current President/Prophet of the LDS Church
Regions: Rapid global growth in Latin America, Africa, Pacific Islands

Name: Gnosticism
Era: 1st-4th century CE; revival in modern era
Description: A diverse collection of ancient religious movements emphasizing secret knowledge (gnosis) as the path to liberation from the material world, often viewing the material world as a flawed creation.
CreationMyth: The true God is hidden, beyond the material world. An inferior divine being (Demiurge) created the flawed material universe. Humans contain a divine spark trapped in material bodies. Sophia (Wisdom), a divine emanation, fell and her fall resulted in the creation of the material world and the Demiurge.
CorePrinciples: Gnosis: Salvific self-knowledge of one's divine nature
The material world is flawed, created by an inferior deity (Demiurge)
A transcendent, unknown God exists beyond the Demiurge
The divine spark within humans seeks return to the Pleroma (divine fullness)
Salvation through knowledge, not faith or works
Dualism: spirit is good, matter is evil or inferior
Hidden teachings transmitted through select initiates

Name: Wicca / Neopaganism
Description: Contemporary pagan religious movements reviving pre-Christian European and nature-based spiritual traditions, emphasizing the divine feminine, magic, and seasonal cycles.
Sources: Aradia: Gospel of the Witches (Charles Godfrey Leland)
CorePrinciples: Divine is immanent in nature and within ourselves
The Goddess and the Horned God as primary divine principles
Wheel of the Year: Eight sabbats marking seasonal cycles
Magic: Directing will and intent to manifest change
Wiccan Rede: An it harm none, do what ye will
Three-fold law: Actions return to the doer threefold
Connection to ancestors, elements, and natural cycles
Personal spiritual experience over dogma
